publication_type: Topic-level evidence synthesis combining classroom IEQ reviews, composite-index methodology papers, school-specific index adaptation studies, and decision-support framing documents.
country_and_climate: The composite-index literature is geographically broad rather than tied to one climate. The classroom-specific evidence used to justify parameters is concentrated in Europe and North America, while recent academic-building reviews expand the geography further. Climate matters because threshold interpretation, weighting, and remediation priority differ between cold, warm, humid, naturally ventilated, and mechanically ventilated settings, even when the index structure is nominally the same.
objective_and_research_question: The central objective is to reduce a multi-dimensional indoor environment into a decision-support representation that remains technically defensible. The key research question is how to combine thermal, acoustic, visual, and air-quality indicators into a composite IEQ or IAQ score, class, or risk index without hiding uncertainty, context, and variable-specific meaning. In schools, a second question is whether such tools can prioritize remediation and communicate conditions better than raw dashboards alone.
study_design: The evidence is mainly methodological and review-based. It includes parameter reviews, conceptual and applied index-development papers, feasibility demonstrations in real buildings, school-specific adaptations of existing schemes, and general reflections on IEQ model construction, weighting, aggregation, and communication. The dominant designs are literature review, analytical framework development, and retrospective application to measured datasets.
educational_context: The school-relevant index literature targets ordinary classrooms in primary and secondary education, with some related evidence from higher-education and broader academic-building environments. The most mature school-specific tool identified in this research set is schoolTAIL, which explicitly adapts a pre-existing IEQ rating scheme to school use. Other tools remain classroom IAQ-specific, building-type generic, or prototype decision frameworks rather than routine institutional standards.
sample_and_duration: [uncertain] The evidence base mixes very different scales. Tran et al. reviewed 88 classroom IEQ measurement papers from the previous decade, while schoolTAIL tested feasibility using measurements from 308 randomly selected schools in a nationwide French survey. Other index papers are proof-of-concept applications in individual buildings or climate-specific classroom scenarios rather than long-running operational school programs. Because many index papers are methodological, monitoring duration is often secondary to index construction.
environmental_variables: Across the literature, the composite IEQ core is stable: thermal conditions, indoor air quality, acoustic conditions, and luminous or visual conditions. Classroom-specific additions include reverberation time and nitrogen dioxide in schoolTAIL, while IAQ-focused indices narrow the scope to pollutants and ventilation-related variables such as CO2, PM2.5, PM10, and context-specific gaseous pollutants. The main design decision is whether the tool is a full IEQ index, an IAQ risk index, or a decision aid tied to one intervention question.
outdoor_conditions_and_baseline: Good index design needs an explicit stance on outdoor context. Full IEQ indices often emphasize indoor state and standards compliance, but classroom interpretation improves when weather, outdoor pollution, and background CO2 are treated as explanatory context or as part of the remediation logic. Without this, a low score may identify a problem without distinguishing whether the dominant driver is outdoor burden, indoor source strength, building operation, or occupancy behavior.
occupancy_and_activity: Occupants shape both the signal and the meaning of a composite index. Classroom density, schedule, age group, teaching activity, voice use, and adaptation behaviors such as window opening affect air quality, acoustics, and comfort simultaneously. Yet many composite tools remain primarily objective and physical, which is one reason the literature keeps returning to questions of weighting and whether occupant perception should modify or complement index scores.
ventilation_and_filtration_operation: Ventilation is central to IAQ-oriented indices and strongly relevant to full IEQ indices, but it is usually represented indirectly through measured outcomes such as CO2, particles, or thermal state rather than as a direct scored variable. This makes the index useful for triage but can weaken causal interpretation if filtration, outdoor pollution episodes, or occupant window behavior are not separately documented. Decision-support tools improve when they expose which remediation lever is implied by the score.
spatial_granularity: Most school-oriented indices are interpreted at classroom or room level, even when the final output is rolled up for a school or building portfolio. That granularity is appropriate because classroom heterogeneity is large and remediation decisions are often room-specific. Portfolio-level indices are still useful for benchmarking and prioritization, but they should be traceable back to room-level components so the user can see which dimension is driving the score.
sensor_specification: Composite IEQ tools do not depend on one hardware brand, but they do depend on obtaining credible measurements for each component. The practical requirement is selective or well-characterized sensing for the most influential channels: true CO2 for ventilation-related IAQ, defensible T/RH for thermal conditions, appropriate acoustic measurements such as noise and reverberation time, illuminance or related visual indicators, and pollutant channels justified by child-health or local building concerns such as PM2.5 or NO2.
calibration_and_qaqc: Index quality is limited by input quality. The classroom review literature shows that no unique standardized measurement method has been used across studies, with inconsistency in duration, location, and reporting. This means any composite score should document calibration state, measurement protocol, sensor limitations, and data cleaning steps explicitly. SchoolTAIL is strong precisely because it starts from parameter choice and threshold classes rather than pretending the measurement layer is already standardized.
acquisition_and_data_quality: For index applications, minute-level acquisition is not always necessary, but consistent temporal aggregation is necessary. A decision-support score should define whether it represents spot conditions, occupied-hour averages, percentile behavior, daily exceedance burden, or longer seasonal summaries. Missing-data handling, QA flags, smoothing rules, and component-specific aggregation windows should be fixed before weighting and scoring, otherwise the index becomes unstable and non-comparable.
sensor_lifecycle: [uncertain] Lifecycle is not a primary concern in most index-development papers, but it matters operationally because component drift can bias weighted scores in ways that are harder to detect than in raw-variable dashboards. Long-lived thermal channels usually create fewer problems than PM modules, optional gas sensors, or acoustical setups that require more careful field maintenance. Any long-term school deployment of an IEQ index therefore still needs the same lifecycle discipline as a raw-monitoring program.
recommended_sensor_by_variable: For school IEQ decision tools, recommend true CO2 by NDIR or photoacoustic NDIR for ventilation-related IAQ, direct T/RH sensing for thermal conditions, optical PM sensing for PM2.5 with caution on PM10, calibrated acoustic measurement including noise and, where possible, reverberation time, and photopic illuminance sensing for visual conditions. Add NO2 only where traffic or combustion relevance justifies it, following the logic used in schoolTAIL. This variable set aligns with the strongest school-specific evidence for composite assessment.
useful_output_and_units: The most defensible outputs are a combination of raw variables and a structured summary. Raw outputs remain CO2 in ppm, temperature in degrees C, RH in percent, PM in micrograms per cubic meter, noise in dBA, reverberation time in seconds, and illuminance in lux. The composite layer can then express these as a class, ordinal level, color code, risk score, or component scorecard, but the raw units must remain visible for diagnosis and action.
direct_measurement_or_proxy: A critical design rule from the model literature is to avoid confusing direct observations with inferred constructs. Thermal and acoustic indicators can be directly measured, while comfort, acceptability, and remediation priority are interpretations. CO2 is directly measured but ventilation adequacy is inferred; PM is measured optically but exposure significance is contextual; and a composite IEQ score is always a constructed proxy for overall indoor quality, not an independent physical quantity.
measurement_principle_and_selectivity: Measurement principles should be chosen to match the role of each component in the index. True CO2 should use selective NDIR or photoacoustic methods, PM relies on optical scattering and therefore needs caution, thermal metrics depend on stable T/RH sensing, and acoustic and visual indices require measurement plans that reflect how classrooms are actually used. The schoolTAIL additions of reverberation time and NO2 are important because they improve selectivity for communication quality and child-relevant pollution burden.
useful_range_and_real_performance: Composite tools should be built around the range where decisions are made, not the nominal maximum range of instruments. School-focused indices need to discriminate ordinary but important classroom variation rather than only detect extreme failures. That means sensitivity around occupied CO2 bands, persistent PM2.5 elevation, thermal discomfort windows, poor acoustics, and inadequate illuminance is more valuable than impressive headline ranges that are rarely reached in real teaching spaces.
operating_regime: The operating regime depends on the purpose of the index. Real-time dashboards may compute rolling component scores continuously, while portfolio benchmarking may run daily, weekly, or seasonal summaries. A useful classroom tool should at least distinguish occupied from unoccupied periods and should avoid scoring startup transients or short sensor anomalies. If the score is used for operational intervention, refresh frequency and persistence logic should be clearly defined.
interferences_and_confounders: The main methodological confounders are weighting choices, compensation effects between components, non-comparable measurement protocols, and hidden assumptions about what counts as acceptable. A room with mediocre scores in all domains may be ranked differently from a room with one severe IAQ problem and otherwise good comfort, depending entirely on aggregation logic. That is why the literature repeatedly stresses transparency of indicator selection, thresholds, and weighting rules.
affordable_validation_protocol: A low-cost validation path for a school IEQ or IAQ index is to validate the component channels first, then validate the index behavior second. First, run short collocation and protocol checks for the core variables. Second, compute the index on a few representative classrooms and test whether the ranking agrees with expert judgment, occupant complaints, and obvious room differences. Third, perform simple sensitivity analysis by changing weights or thresholds to see whether the prioritization is stable enough for decision use.
validation_metrics: Component-level metrics should include the usual bias, MAE, RMSE, slope, intercept, and uptime where sensors are involved. Index-level metrics should include rank stability, sensitivity to weights and thresholds, agreement with expert or auditor classification, percentage of rooms reclassified by protocol choices, and whether the tool supports consistent remediation priority. For risk indices, confusion between categories should be reported rather than only one global score.
installation_and_enclosure: Because the index is downstream from measurement, the installation plan should follow the needs of the dominant components. Classroom nodes should be placed at representative room locations and heights, while acoustic and illuminance assessment may require more deliberate protocols than a single fixed environmental monitor. If one composite score is intended, the installation metadata must be detailed enough to justify that the contributing measurements are representative of the same occupied environment.
hardware_integration: Hardware integration for composite tools is straightforward when they are built on an existing classroom monitoring stack. The main requirement is that all channels share synchronized timestamps, stable metadata, and reproducible preprocessing so the index is computed on comparable inputs. If the tool mixes measurements, simulation, and visual observation as TAIL does, the software layer must store the provenance of each component rather than treating every input as equivalent sensor data.
total_implementation_cost: [uncertain] Composite scoring itself is cheap in software, but credible implementation still inherits the cost of the underlying monitoring program and the labor needed to define, test, explain, and maintain the score. A classroom IAQ risk index may be relatively inexpensive if it uses an existing sensor stack, whereas a full school IEQ index becomes more costly when it adds acoustics, illuminance protocol, NO2, or simulation and observation inputs. The index is therefore rarely the main cost driver; scope and measurement ambition are.
evidence_maturity: Evidence maturity is moderate for the general idea of composite IEQ and IAQ decision tools, high for the need to assess multiple IEQ dimensions jointly, and still evolving for school-specific operational deployment. TAIL is a mature and well-documented methodological foundation, schoolTAIL is a strong recent school adaptation, and IAQ-only classroom risk indices are emerging. The weakest point remains external validation across climates, pedagogies, and institutional workflows.
variable_specific_cautions: A composite score can hide the very variable that requires urgent action. CO2 can dominate user attention even when particles, NO2, noise, or reverberation are the more important classroom issue. PM10 from compact sensors should be treated cautiously, subjective comfort should not be confused with pollutant burden, and weighting schemes copied from offices may not transfer cleanly to children and teaching activities. The score should therefore be read as a decision aid, not as a complete diagnosis.
system_architecture: A useful architecture for composite decision tools is raw classroom sensing plus metadata storage plus a transparent scoring layer plus a visualization layer that shows both components and total class. The scoring engine should store the chosen thresholds, weights, aggregation rules, and versioning so that a room score can be reproduced later. If remediation planning is in scope, the architecture should also map low-scoring components to recommended actions rather than just to a numeric grade.
connectivity_and_protocols: There is no special protocol requirement for index computation beyond reliable collection of the component variables. Wi-Fi, LoRaWAN, MQTT, HTTPS, and ordinary time-series storage are all compatible. The more important architectural requirement is schema stability so that the same index can be recomputed after software changes or across multiple schools without ambiguity in units, occupied-state handling, or QA flags.
interoperability_and_data_model: The data model should keep component variables, contextual metadata, and composite outputs separate. At minimum it should encode room ID, time window, variable, unit, preprocessing status, threshold set, index version, component score, and overall score or class. For methods like TAIL and schoolTAIL, the model should also support mixed input types such as measurement, observation, and simulation. This separation is essential for explainability and auditability.
cybersecurity_privacy_and_ethics: Composite IEQ tools usually pose less privacy risk than camera-heavy occupancy systems, but they still influence decisions about room quality, maintenance urgency, and institutional reputation. Governance matters because a low score can trigger public concern or resource allocation consequences. Ethical use therefore requires transparent methods, cautious communication, and avoidance of false precision, especially when school scores may shape investment priorities across unequal campuses.
analytical_methods: The core analytical tasks are indicator selection, threshold definition, normalization, weighting, aggregation, sensitivity analysis, and visualization. TAIL and schoolTAIL explicitly operationalize multi-domain classification with color and Roman-numeral classes, while low-cost monitoring platforms and IAQ risk indices show how continuous sensor data can feed dynamic scoring. The model literature also emphasizes that validation and interpretability are not optional extras; they are part of the method.
derived_index_or_model: A composite IEQ or IAQ index is itself the main derived model. TAIL rates thermal, acoustic, indoor-air, and luminous environments and then combines them into an overall IEQ class. SchoolTAIL retains this structure but adds reverberation time and NO2 and updates PM2.5 classes to align with the 2021 WHO guidelines. IAQ-specific classroom tools narrow the focus and can be used when the decision problem is ventilation and pollution risk rather than overall classroom environmental quality.
decision_rules_and_standards: The strongest decision-support schemes in this set derive their classes from explicit standards and guideline references rather than arbitrary cutoffs. TAIL relies primarily on EN-16798-1 and WHO air-quality guidelines, and schoolTAIL updates PM2.5 quality classes and adds school-relevant parameters to strengthen classroom applicability. CSTB also frames index construction in three steps: choose relevant fields and thresholds, define aggregation rules, and define a result display paired with recommended actions. This is a sound blueprint for any classroom decision tool.
intervention_and_automation: Composite tools are most defensible as prioritization and communication aids rather than as fully automated controllers. Their strongest use is to identify whether a classroom needs ventilation improvement, acoustic treatment, shading or lighting change, filtration, or broader renovation. Automation can consume component scores as inputs, but direct actuation should still rely on the underlying measured variables because a single overall score is too coarse to control building systems safely.
environmental_outcomes: The direct outcome of a good composite tool is clearer prioritization of IEQ problems across rooms or schools. SchoolTAIL explicitly demonstrated feasibility for identifying potential problems and prioritizing IEQ remediations in 308 French schools, while TAIL showed that a structured rating can discriminate IEQ levels across different buildings. The environmental benefit comes when this prioritization results in targeted interventions rather than passive reporting.
health_and_learning_outcomes: [uncertain] The rationale for composite classroom indices is strongly linked to health, comfort, and learning, but the evidence base still supports this mainly indirectly. A better score should help identify rooms likely to undermine well-being or learning conditions, yet direct causal evidence that adopting one composite tool improves student outcomes more than simpler monitoring remains limited. This is a promising but not fully validated benefit pathway.
objective_subjective_integration: One of the unresolved model questions is how objective measurements should interact with subjective experience. Many IEQ tools are still heavily objective, but the broader literature shows that satisfaction and adaptation do not always align with standards-based thresholds. The best current practice is to keep measured component scores primary while allowing occupant feedback, complaints, or comfort surveys to contextualize or challenge the interpretation.
quantitative_results: [uncertain] The most concrete quantitative classroom evidence in this source set is structural rather than outcome-based: Tran et al. reviewed 88 classroom IEQ papers, TAIL used 12 parameters and demonstrated discrimination across 11 European buildings, and schoolTAIL was tested for feasibility using 308 schools in France while adding reverberation time and NO2. Mujan et al. also reported less than 3 percent data loss in a low-cost monitoring platform used to support an IEQ dashboard. What remains less established is a universal performance benchmark showing that one composite index consistently predicts superior classroom outcomes across regions and school types.
feasibility_and_acceptance: [uncertain] Feasibility is good when the tool is transparent, component-based, and built on an existing monitoring workflow. Acceptance is likely higher for schoolTAIL-style class systems and color codes than for opaque weighted scores, but systematic user-acceptance evidence in school operations is still limited. In practice, facilities staff are more likely to trust a composite tool when they can inspect the contributing variables and understand the implied action.
validity_and_limitations: The main validity challenge is that every composite tool encodes judgment. Indicator choice, thresholds, normalization, and weighting all affect the result. Compensation between domains can mask severe single-variable failures, and school transferability is limited when the model was calibrated or conceptualized for other building types or climates. The safest use is decision support with transparent components, not replacement of the raw measurement record.
contribution_and_research_gaps: The most important current contribution is that the field has moved from generic calls for holistic IEQ toward actual school-adapted decision tools. TAIL provides a rigorous multi-domain foundation, schoolTAIL shows how to adapt it to classrooms, and newer IAQ risk tools and sustainability-oriented frameworks expand the design space. The main gaps are stronger school-side validation, explicit treatment of uncertainty and equity, better integration of subjective response, and longitudinal evidence that composite scoring changes remediation choices and outcomes more effectively than simpler room-level dashboards.
